section_1.title: The Dimensional Paradox (0:00-0:45)
section_1.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept: A 1D line has length, and a 2D plane has area. Pose the question: Can a continuous line pass through every single point in a 2D square? Challenge the intuition that a line has 'zero area'.
section_1.example: Visualize a thin thread moving across a square grid; show how it can never fill the 'gaps' until it infinitely twists.

section_2.title: The Peano Curve Construction (0:45-2:00)
section_2.content: Explain the recursive algorithm. Start with a square grid (1x1), subdivide into 9 smaller squares, and trace a path through them. Show that as the iteration count 'n' approaches infinity, the path effectively covers all points.
section_2.example: An animation of a 'snake-like' path subdividing into smaller segments, demonstrating how complexity increases with each iteration step.

section_3.title: The Hilbert Curve: Efficiency in Recursion (2:00-3:15)
section_3.content: Introduce the Hilbert curve as a more popular alternative to Peano. Explain the 'L-shape' rotation logic. Emphasize that it is continuous, surjective, and maintains locality (points close together on the line are close in the 2D space).
section_3.example: A visual comparison: Hilbert curve vs. a random scribble, showing how the Hilbert curve maps a 1D sequence to a 2D layout without 'jumping' across distant areas.

section_4.title: Real-World Applications (3:15-4:30)
section_4.content: Explain why this matters: Database indexing (mapping 2D geographical data to 1D disk storage), image processing, and fractal antenna design. Explain that 'locality' helps computers read data faster.
section_4.example: A 'Pixel-sorting' robot character moving along a Hilbert path to organize scattered colored dots into a coherent image efficiently.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Intuitive Summary (4:30-5:00)
section_5.content: Summarize the key takeaway: Space-filling curves are infinite limits of simple patterns that allow us to 'flatten' dimensions. Encouraging students to see fractals as nature's way of maximizing surface area.
section_5.example: A final graphic showing a human lung or a fern leaf, highlighting how nature uses space-filling principles to pack maximum surface area into minimal volume.
